extracted.intended_audience: logicians, philosophers, scientific and technical writers, and scholars concerned with terminology and the philosophy of language
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance for creating and maintaining a language (terminology) suitable for philosophical and scientific inquiry: ensure terms are determinate, descriptive, appropriately coined, and historically informed. Emphasizes descriptive terminology, conventions tied to perception, and the dangers of casual semantic change.

rubrics_metrics.name: Know the history of a term before altering its meaning
rubrics_metrics.description: Whoever seeks to introduce a more correct use of a term with important associations should possess an accurate acquaintance with the history of the particular word, and of the opinions which in different stages of its progress it served to express.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: To be qualified to define a name, know all that has ever been known of the properties of the class denoted. If a new meaning would render false any proposition that was ever generally held true, you must be sure you have considered everything those earlier users understood. Historical familiarity prevents inadvertent loss of important premises; revisions should not make previously accepted truths false by changing terms.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prefer a word’s history over its dictionary entry when prescribing usage
rubrics_metrics.description: The dictionary meaning is a broad, blunt exponent of a word's real meaning; the history of a word, by showing causes which determine its use, is often a better guide to its employment than any definition.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Dictionaries often miss collateral associations and subtle shades. For words in common use, consult their historical development to understand the law of their semantic succession; this helps to anticipate connotations and proper contexts of use.

rubrics_metrics.name: Account for connotation formed by habitual associated circumstances
rubrics_metrics.description: A common-name’s connotation is derived from the circumstances habitually brought to mind when it is pronounced; casual circumstances that often co-occur with the referent can become part of its connotation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Be aware that properties casually associated with named objects (social context, typical circumstances) can become part of meaning; such associations explain why near-synonyms are not interchangeable in all contexts. When choosing terms, consider habitual associative contexts as well as core properties.

rubrics_metrics.name: Recognize and manage the twin processes of generalization and specialization
rubrics_metrics.description: Language undergoes two counter-movements: generalization (words losing portions of connotation and becoming more general) and specialization (words acquiring new connotation and becoming restricted).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Expect words to broaden or narrow in meaning over time. Track these tendencies (e.g., 'pagan' becoming 'heathen', 'villain' shifting to moral sense). In designing terminology, guard against unwanted drift by clear conventions; when drift is irreversible, document both old and new senses.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid semantic degeneration by ignorant or careless misuse
rubrics_metrics.description: Frequent ignorant misuse widens a word’s use beyond its proper meaning, contributing to degeneration of language and loss of modes of expressing thought.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Watch for vulgarisms and careless extensions (examples: 'transpire' used for 'happen', 'aggravating' for 'provoking', misuse of 'alone' as 'only', confusion of 'predicate'/'predict', reversed sense of 'eliminate'). Such corruptions narrow precision and force circumlocution. Editors and authors should resist and correct these usages where clarity matters.

rubrics_metrics.name: Provide names for all important meanings (no important meaning without a word)
rubrics_metrics.description: Not only should every word perfectly express its meaning, but there should be no important meaning without its word: whatever we have occasion to think of often and for scientific purposes ought to have a name.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A philosophical/scientific language must include terms for any recurring or important concept so that thought and record are possible with precision and brevity. Where no distinct name exists, coin or fix one by convention.

rubrics_metrics.name: Establish an accurate descriptive terminology for observable properties
rubrics_metrics.description: There ought to be all such names as are needful for making a record of individual observations so the words of the record exactly show what fact has been observed.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: For sciences concerned with external objects, create names for elementary sensations and for frequently recurring combinations. Descriptive vocabulary should allow one to record specific observed facts unambiguously (e.g., botanical terms naming parts and forms).

rubrics_metrics.name: Fix technical terms by convention and tie them directly to perception
rubrics_metrics.description: The meaning of descriptive technical terms can be fixed in the first instance only by convention and can be made intelligible only by presenting to the senses that which the terms are to signify.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Teach technical terms through immediate association with the perception (e.g., color swatches for 'apple-green' or 'French gray') so that the term evokes the sensation without conjecture. Avoid relying on vague common-language bridges when precision is required.

rubrics_metrics.name: Elementary sensations cannot be defined verbally; teach by experience
rubrics_metrics.description: The names of elementary sensations or elementary feelings cannot be defined; their signification is known only by making the learner experience the sensation or by referring him to a remembered perception.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use direct demonstration or standard exemplars for basic sensory terms rather than verbal definitions. Reserve verbal definitions for compound or higher-level notions that can be decomposed into named elements.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use defined compound terms for frequently recurring combinations
rubrics_metrics.description: Combinations of sensations or feelings may be described if there is a name for each elementary feeling; brevity and clearness are promoted by giving distinctive names also to combinations of frequent recurrence.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Introduce compound technical names (e.g., 'papilionaceous' describing a specific petal arrangement) where a recurring complex pattern exists; define them precisely so they can be used without ambiguity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Adopt numerical and unambiguous standards where appropriate
rubrics_metrics.description: When possible, introduce numerical or clearly bounded definitions (examples: leaf forms distinguished by precise relations; siliqua defined as a pod four times as long as broad; Mohs hardness scale; Werner’s color scale).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Where properties admit quantification or ordinal ranking, use numeric scales or precise ratios to avoid vagueness. This aids reproducibility and communication across practitioners.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prefer creating new names rather than forcing old names to cover novel objects
rubrics_metrics.description: When the number of things we know multiplies faster than names, it is natural to give a new object a name which expresses its resemblance to something known, but it is often better to introduce a new name than to overextend an existing one.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid turning species names into genera indiscriminately; where a genuinely new kind requires distinct treatment, coin or agree on a specific term to preserve clarity of classification and avoid ambiguity (illustrated by 'salt', 'oil', 'glass' becoming generic).

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid question-begging names that embed value judgments
rubrics_metrics.description: Many names that express moral or social facts carry a connotation of approbation or censure, producing the fallacy of 'question-begging names'—the predicate under inquiry is assumed by the term itself.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Monitor and avoid using terms that presuppose the very property to be proved (Bentham’s critique). Where such emotive connotations exist, either neutralize the term or define it explicitly to separate descriptive content from evaluative stance.

rubrics_metrics.name: When semantic change is irrevocable, redefine & retain former sense as secondary
rubrics_metrics.description: If transformations in meaning are irrevocably effected, the logician should submit and, if a definition is necessary, define the word according to its new meaning; retain the former meaning as a second signification if needed.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Recognize when usage has permanently shifted; adopt contemporary meaning for working definitions while documenting and preserving old senses where philosophically or historically important. This pragmatic flexibility prevents futile resistance to established usage while preserving continuity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Logicians can’t make meanings for common words but can clarify them
rubrics_metrics.description: Logicians cannot make the meaning of any but scientific terms; the meaning of other words is made by the collective human race. But logicians can ascertain what has guided general employment of a name and clothe it in distinct terms.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Focus logicians’ efforts on analyzing causes of prevailing usage and formalizing those usages into clear, permanent definitions where feasible. Use such clarified formulations to teach and stabilize the sense within philosophy or science.
